prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms brought optical frequency standards to a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B061 alone, Katori and Ye. After the first round I tested it against the chair's novelty question and I think it holds on scientific grounds. The 2005 prize honoured the frequency comb, a counting tool. The 2012 prize honoured quantum control of single trapped systems, where a single ion gives an excellent clock but very low signal-to-noise. The lattice clock is a different principle: Katori's magic-wavelength condition cancels the lattice light shift for the clock transition, so thousands of neutral atoms can be held tightly and interrogated in parallel with no first-order perturbation. That is what turned a single-particle precision idea into one with the statistics needed for 10^-18, and it is what separates it from the ion-clock line. The experimental record is what I trust most as an instrument builder: blackbody, lattice, collisional and density shifts each identified and measured, and clocks in Japan, the US, Germany, France and China compared directly with one another. The credit is compact and the two roles are clear, Katori for the concept and first realisation, Ye for taking strontium to the systematic floor with the many-body and cavity-enhanced work. The consequences are already realised: tests of the constancy of constants and dark-matter couplings, centimetre-scale relativistic geodesy. I do not count the pending redefinition of the second for or against the timing; it is a metrology decision and the physics stands without it.
statement.case_against: The objection I cannot fully remove is that this sits in a line of precision-spectroscopy prizes (2005, 2012) and is an engineering-physics achievement more than a new phenomenon, as Kroll says himself. Narrow wording helps but does not erase the credit boundary: Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Hinkley, Takamoto, Bloom and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups produced essential parts of the 10^-18 result, and any two-name prize draws a line through a contested field. If the committee wants a discovery of new matter rather than a measurement capability, B013 is the stronger answer, and B013 has an experimental claim to originality that a clock cannot match. I also have to say plainly that I am a particle and astroparticle physicist and am judging atomic-physics credit with the help of Kroll and Lindroth.

responses.point: Kroll holds that a lattice-clock prize is an engineering-physics achievement, not a new phenomenon, and that the citation must be worded narrowly for the lattice clock.
responses.response: I have adopted your narrow wording in my citation and I think it largely answers the chair's novelty objection: the citation names the invention and realisation of the lattice clock and the 10^-18 result it enabled, and does not claim optical clocks as a field. It does not answer the objection that this is a measurement capability and not a new phenomenon. I accept that, and I would say it openly. My view is that a detector or instrument that opens a regime nobody could reach, with independent reproduction, is within the mandate for an invention that improves physics, and in physics that is not a lesser category. I agree with you that the redefinition of the second should not count either way.

responses.point: Lindroth sees the many-atom magic-wavelength lattice as a genuine conceptual step beyond single-ion clocks and treats the redefinition of the second as a consequence, not a motivation.
responses.response: Your argument is the one I rely on for the novelty question, since I cannot judge atomic physics at your level. The distinction I take from you is that the comb gave a counting tool, the 2012 work gave control of one quantum system, and the lattice gives parallel interrogation without a first-order light shift, which is what makes the statistics possible. If you or Kroll think that is overstated, please say so now. I also take your point that Ye's earlier comb work was already rewarded; in the citation I credit him only for the lattice-clock precision work, not for the comb.

responses.point: Olsson reads the mandate as favouring an experimentally verified discovery with an original experiment, wants certainty that the credited people did the original work in B013, and ranks B013 close to first.
responses.response: I read the mandate as covering both, and I think a clock with every systematic identified and measured is as well verified as anything on our list. I do not agree that B061 lacks an original experiment: Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and first strontium clock are exactly that. On B013, I share your wish to be certain about the original credit and I cannot resolve the Yuan Cao and early band-structure question from the record, which is why I will not push the committee toward B013 without that being settled. If the experts conclude the experimental credit sits clearly with Jarillo-Herrero's group, I could accept B013 and would not block it.

responses.point: Mehlig asks whether the members who ranked B061 first would prefer it on maturity grounds, and says B013 is early if the pairing mechanism must be understood first.
responses.response: Yes, maturity is part of why I prefer B061, and it is the main place I differ from you. The 10^-18 result is reproduced between independent laboratories and the systematic budgets are published and cross-checked. I accept the point you and Danielsson both make that B013 does not depend on the pairing mechanism: it is the platform and the correlated phases that were discovered. I would not make the mechanism the test. My test is whether a result has been confirmed independently and has lasted, and B013 meets the first, while the second is still being tested at under a decade. So I weigh timing, not merit, in B061's favour.

responses.point: Eriksson sees B013 as clean theory-experiment closure, but worries that a second condensed-matter prize after 2016, and a recent 2025 circuit prize, could shift the committee toward an AMO or precision choice.
responses.response: I defer to you on the physics of B013, and I do not think recent prizes in neighbouring areas should decide the matter: each case should stand on its own merits. I would note the point you raise is a mild consideration for B061 only, since 2025 went to superconducting circuits, which is a different community from atomic clocks. Your own list has B061 as an alternative, and my answer to the chair's question is the same in reverse: you could accept B061, and I could accept B013 on condition that the attribution question for Cao and the earlier theorists is settled by the experts and the committee is content with the maturity.

responses.point: Johansson moved to B061 from circuit QED, raises a combined prize with B034, and notes the SI redefinition is still pending.
responses.response: I welcome the move, and I agree with you that breadth of support across different backgrounds says something, though I would not rest the case on it. On a combination with B034, I do not think the three-person limit allows it without dropping a name: B061 uses two and B034 uses two. I would not cut Katori or Ye to make room, since the credit is cleanest as a pair. A single-part B061 is my proposal. On the redefinition, as with Kroll, I would not let it count for or against timing.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the lattice clock is a distinct step from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes; I have argued it is but I rely on Kroll and Lindroth for the atomic physics.
Whether Katori and Ye are the right two names given Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow, Hinkley, Takamoto and Bloom; I am working from memory and cannot check the historical record beyond the supplied names.
Whether the committee prefers a precision-measurement achievement or a discovery in quantum matter this year; I could accept B013 if its attribution and maturity questions were settled.
Whether B009 will gain independent source confirmation, which would change my view of it for a later year.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict for B061 or B013 from my profile. For disclosure: I am a member of the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations. Fermi-LAT took part in multimessenger follow-up of IceCube alerts, so there is mild field proximity to B009, and my cosmic-ray antimatter background is adjacent to B005. I have no direct connection to any credited person and neither B009 nor B005 is my preferred part.
